content.title: Author Response to Reviewer s5AT
content.comment:
We appreciate your questions and comments on our work. We have left comments on each question.

Q: The paper lacks a clear definition of what is meant by similarity of sentences.

In semantic textual similarity (STS), similarity between sentences is defined as meaning similarity (semantic similarity) between sentences. The meaning similarity of two sentences is determined by the degree of details shared between the sentences. Previous STS studies provide the guideline for determining similarity scores between sentences; “SemEval-2017 Task 1: Semantic Textual Similarity Multilingual and Cross-lingual Focused Evaluation” and “SEM 2013 shared task: Semantic Textual Similarity”. For example, when two sentences have the completely same meaning, their similarity score is 5 and when two sentences are mostly equivalent but different on unimportant details, then their similarity score is 4. We will provide a more clear definition in our paper.

Q: The motivation is that current sentence encoders have difficulty in learning fine-grained semantic differences. The author claim to have proposed a method that solves this problem. How is their claim evaluated?

We evaluate this claim in Figure 7. The STS performance on similar sentences highlights sentence encoders’ ability to capture fine-grained semantic differences since similar sentences have small semantic differences. Figure 7 shows the STS performances of our model and baselines on a dataset that consists of similar sentence pairs. We show that our method outperforms baselines on similar sentence pairs.

Q: The work relies on the neighbor sentences and assumes that these sentences approximate the fine-grained semantic properties of seed sentences. It is not clear how.

We will clarify how our approach leverages its neighbor sentences. Our approach infers the semantic meaning of an input sentence with the prior distribution of the semantic vector space approximated by its neighbor sentences. Sentence vectors are not uniformly distributed in the vector space since some semantic meanings are more/less used in the corpus. Figure 8a shows an approximation of the prior distribution of semantic meanings used in the corpus; we can see sentence vectors as samples drawn from the prior distribution of the semantic space. Thus, when an input sentence is near some sentence vectors that are densely distributed (cluster), there is a high chance that the semantic meaning of the input sentence is also similar to the semantic meaning of that cluster. Our approach leverages the prior distribution approximated by its neighbor sentences.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer DPxP
content.comment:
We appreciate your comments on our work. We addressed all your questions and comments below.

Q: It'll be interesting and more convincing to see how well the proposed model does on other downstream tasks, e.g. natural language inference, sentiment analysis.

Thank you for the great comment. We report the performances of RankEncoder on other downstream tasks in the following table. These seven transfer tasks are standard tasks for measuring the performance of sentence encoders.

| Model              |     MR    |     CR    |    SUBJ   |    MPQA   |    SST    |    TREC   |    MRPC   |    AVG    |
|--------------------|:---------:|:---------:|:---------:|:---------:|:---------:|:---------:|:---------:|:---------:|
| SimCSE             |   81.18   |   86.46   |   94.45   |   88.88   |   85.50   |   89.80   |   74.43   |   85.81   |
| SimCSE w/ MLM      | **82.92** |   87.23   | **95.71** |   88.73   | **86.81** |   87.01   | **78.07** |   86.64   |
| RankEncoder-SimCSE |   82.14   | **87.31** |   95.35   | **89.05** |   86.66   | **91.00** |   76.06   | **86.80** |

We haven’t attached this result to our paper since there is no direct connection between transfer tasks and sentence embedding performance. The paper “SimCSE: Simple Contrastive Learning of Sentence Embeddings,” which brought a significant breakthrough in this field, states that “confirming our intuition that sentence-level objective may not directly benefit transfer tasks” (The second paragraph in Section E Transfer Tasks). As a result, recent unsupervised sentence representation learning studies often skip evaluating their sentence encoder on transfer tasks, e.g., “PromptBERT: Improving BERT Sentence Embeddings with Prompts, EMNLP 2022.”
We will add these results and more analysis on transfer tasks in our paper.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer Pwq7
content.comment:
We appreciate your comments on our work. We addressed all your questions and comments below.

Q: It is highly desired to analyze the performance-efficiency trade-off of the proposed method.

This is a great question. Performance-efficiency trade-off is an important problem in the semantic textual similarity field. We measured the computational efficiency of RankEncoder, and this only requires 1.8% additional inference time than the inference time of previous approaches. I’ll describe more about our computation below.

The proposed method computes the rank vector of an input sentence by computing similarity scores between the input sentence and all sentences in the corpus, not between every pair of sentences in the corpus. We only need to compute the inner product between the $d$-dimension vector (the vector of an input sentence) and $d \times n$ matrix (vectors of $n$ sentences in the corpus); where $d$ is the size of the dimension. Thus, the time complexity for computing a single rank vector is $O(n \times d \times d) $ when we have $n$ sentences in the corpus.
Also, the sentence embedding vectors of all sentences in the corpus can be pre-computed after training stage, and this does not affect the inference time.
Overall, the inference process consists of 1) generating the sentence vector of an input sentence and 2) computing similarity scores between the input sentence vector and the pre-computed $n$ sentence vectors ($n$ is set as 10,0000 in our study) of the corpus. The second step takes only negligible computation time, 1.8% of the whole inference time; the first step (sentence embedding step) takes 0.07 seconds, and the second step takes 0.0013 seconds on a single RTX 8000 GPU. (0.0013 seconds / 0.0713 seconds == 0.018)

Q: Is there any standard that can be applied for determining the values of $\tau_l$ and $\tau_r$? In terms of reproducibility, the authors need to more clarify how to decide $\lambda_{inf}$, $\tau_r$, and $\tau_l$. And I'm also interested in what will happen if we do not apply the pair filtering mechanism.

We will add more description about this. Our model is actually not sensitive to the choices of $\tau_l$ and $\tau_r$. We have chosen the values of these hyperparameters with grid search over validation set performance; we adjusted these two hyperparameters and found the best-performing values.

Sentence pair filtering brings little performance improvement. We use this strategy to push the performance boundary as much as possible. RankEncoder’s AVG performance is 79.90 without the sentence filtering strategy, which is a 0.17%p lower spearman correlation compared to the RankEncoder with the sentence pair filtering strategy (80.07 spearman correlation). We will add an ablation study on sentence pair filtering in the revision.

Q: In Section 5.4, why is it desirable to have more distant distances between positive pairs? While it improves uniformity, it will also reduce alignment. I'm wondering why the authors only consider uniformity, excluding alignment.

We report the alignment scores in the following table. We will add these results to our paper. As an alternative of alignment, we show the STS performance of our approach on positive sentence pairs; in Figure 7, we show that our approach captures the similarity scores between positive sentence pairs better than baselines. We use this metric instead of alignment because identifying closer sentence pairs (relative distance) is more important than measuring the absolute distance between sentences.

| Model                  | Uniformity | Alignment |
|------------------------|:----------:|:---------:|
| SimCSE                 |    -2.42   |    0.21   |
| RankEncoder-SimCSE     |    -3.23   |    0.23   |
| PromptBERT             |    -1.49   |    0.11   |
| RankEncoder-PromptBERT |    -3.31   |    0.22   |
| SNCSE                  |    -2.21   |    0.16   |
| RankEncoder-SNCSE      |    -3.20   |    0.21   |

Also, we report the uniformity of our approach to empirically verify the mathematical property of RankEncoder discussed in Section 3.3. In Section 3.3, we show that increased uniformity is one of the consequences of applying our approach to other sentence encoders; in Figure 4, we illustrated that densely distributed semantic space is expanded and more distinguishable by our rank vectors. We verify this property in Figure 8 by displaying the real semantic vector space of a base encoder and the semantic vector space of our approach, and we provide more details of Figure 8 in Table 4.

content.title: General Response to Reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their thoughtful comments. The main contributions of our work as the reviewers acknowledge are:

1. Our approach achieved consistent improvement from the previous state-of-the-art models’ STS performance (Reviewer Pwq7, DW6a, DPxP).

2. Our approach is generally applicable to any other unsupervised sentence encoder (Reviewer Pwq7, DW6a).

3. This paper proposes a novel direction for sentence representation learning that is not covered by previous approaches. Most previous approaches focus on developing data augmentation methods for contrastive learning, but our approach infers the semantic meaning of an input sentence from its neighbor sentences (Reviewer DW6a, DPxP).

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a ranking-based approach for improving the quality of unsupervised sentence representations (most of which are already tuned using contrastive learning).

Given a temporary sentence encoder ($E_1$), one computes the embeddings of all sentences in a corpus using the encoder and based on this information, derives a ranking vector for each sentence that contains similarity scores between the target sentence and all the other sentences.

The ranking vectors are then utilized for training the final encoder ($E_2$) such that the dot product of the ranking vectors of a pair of sentences should be close to the cosine similarity of the representations of the two sentences.

This approach has merits in that it is applicable to any other unsupervised sentence representation learning methods and that it brings a moderate amount of improvement when evaluated on Semantic Textual Similarity tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- The proposed method is widely applicable, giving a moderate amount of improvement when applied to other methods for unsupervised learning of sentence representations.
- The authors present a series of intuitive examples and reasoning that can help readers to better understand why the proposed method is effective.

Weaknesses
- It is highly desired to analyze the performance-efficiency trade-off of the proposed method. It seems that the computational cost required for the proposed method is relatively heavy, even though the method provides a moderate amount of improvement in the final performance. Theoretically, computing the similarity of every pair of sentences in a corpus of size $n$ requires an algorithm whose complexity is $O(n^2)$. If so, why don't we just employ a cross-encoder (whose complexity is also $O(n^2)$) that accepts a pair of sentences at the same time rather than deriving the representation of each sentence separately? In the SBERT paper (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019), the aforementioned problem was considered as one of the main motivations for why we need to develop sentence encoders that individually encode each sentence rather than processing a pair of sentences at the same time. Considering this, I'm not sure the proposed method guarantees a good balance in terms of a performance-efficiency trade-off.
- There exist some hyperparameters whose selection can be somewhat arbitrary. Is there any standard that can be applied for determining the values of $\tau_{l}$ and $\tau_{r}$? I believe that the pair filtering mechanism would significantly impact the final performance, so it should be clarified how we can decide optimal values for the hyperparameters.
I also suspect that we can also gain some improvement when directly applying the same mechanism to the existing contrastive learning-based approaches for sentence representations.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Most of the content presented in the paper is clear, but there is room for improvement, e.g., In Section 5.4, why is it desirable to have more distant distances between positive pairs? While it improves uniformity, it will also reduce alignment. I'm wondering why the authors only consider uniformity, excluding alignment.
- In terms of reproducibility, the authors need to more clarify how to decide $\lambda_{inf}$, $\tau_{l}$, and $\tau_{r}$. And I'm also interested in what will happen if we do not apply the pair filtering mechanism.
content.summary_of_the_review:
In summary, the paper presents an intuitive and widely applicable method for improving the quality of sentence representations based on unsupervised learning.
However, I believe that its performance-efficiency trade-off should be seriously considered, considering that the proposed method takes a two-stage learning algorithm and that it requires computations between every pair of sentences in a corpus.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
What is the goal of the paper?

* Ranking-enhanced unsupervised sentence representation learning


What has been done before?

* Previous unsupervised sentence encoders based on data augmentation methods have a certain limitation for capturing fine-grained semantic meanings of sentences. Compared to previous approaches focused on generating better positive and negative pairs, this work uses neighbor sentences to get more accurate supervision signals for similar sentence pairs, which is a novel approach that previous approaches have not covered.


What are the contributions of the paper?

* Demonstrated that previous contrastive learning approaches based on data augmentation methods are limited for capturing fine-grained semantic differences, leading to a large performance difference between unsupervised and supervised methods

* Proposed RankEncoder, which uses relations between an input sentence and sentences in a corpus for training unsupervised sentence encoders. It leverages neighbor sentences for capturing fine-grained semantic differences.

* Evaluated RankEncoder from three perspectives and achieved SOTA results: 1) the semantic textual similarity performance, 2) the efficacy on similar sentence pairs, and 3) the universality of RankEncoder 

* Source code of RankEncoder is available

What are the main results?

* Experimental results on seven STS benchmark datasets show that RankEncoder achieves 80.07% Spearman’s correlation, a 1.1% absolute improvement compared to the previous state-of-the-art performance. The improvement is even more significant, a 1.73% improvement, on similar sentence pairs. Also, they demonstrate that RankEncoder is universally applicable to existing unsupervised sentence encoders


Why would techniques developed in this project benefit others?

* RankEncoder is generally applicable to any unsupervised sentence encoder.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

* SOTA results on STS performance especially on similar sentence pairs and thus, reduced the gap between supervised and unsupervised sentence encoders

* RankEncoder is generally applicable to any unsupervised sentence encoder

* Source code of RankEncoder is available

How is their claim evaluated? The absolute improvement compared to previous state-of-the-art performance for several datasets is still low. 

The work relies on the neighbor sentences and assumes that these sentences approximate the fine-grained semantic properties of seed sentences. It is not clear how. The neighbor sentences might provide additional context to resolve ambiguity, but fine-grained semantics refer to attributes and relationships of the objects mentioned in the sentence and to find neighbor sentences that express the same attributes and relationships of objects is not guaranteed with the method proposed. 

To find neighbor sentences the proposed model already relies on a representation of the sentences and a similarity metric. It is not guaranteed that this representation has the necessary properties to retrieve useful sentences to augment the training and noise could be introduced. 

Please clarify the scaling of the two terms of which the squared difference is taken in equations 4 and 7.

content.title: Ranking-Enhanced Unsupervised Sentence Representation Learning
content.abstract: Previous unsupervised sentence embedding studies have focused on data augmentation methods such as dropout masking and rule-based sentence transformation methods. However, these approaches have a limitation of controlling the fine-grained semantics of augmented views of a sentence. This results in inadequate supervision signals for capturing a semantic similarity of similar sentences. In this work, we found that using neighbor sentences enables capturing a more accurate semantic similarity between similar sentences. Based on this finding, we propose RankEncoder, which uses relations between an input sentence and sentences in a corpus for training unsupervised sentence encoders. We evaluate RankEncoder from three perspectives: 1) the semantic textual similarity performance, 2) the efficacy on similar sentence pairs, and 3) the universality of RankEncoder. Experimental results show that RankEncoder achieves 80.07% Spearman's correlation, a 1.1% absolute improvement compared to the previous state-of-the-art performance. The improvement is even more significant, a 1.73% improvement, on similar sentence pairs. Also, we demonstrate that RankEncoder is universally applicable to existing unsupervised sentence encoders.
